final_text:
I edited two rows of the token-embedding matrix, and the model now does the task zero-shot. Training-set accuracy went from 0% to **87.5% (14/16)**, measured with the real evaluation pipeline (`eval_train`, 6 new tokens). I used 40 of the 50 forward passes.

**What I changed**
- The row for the token `Input` (id 2505) is now a copy of the row for `English` (id 22574).
- The row for the token `Output` (id 5097) is now a copy of the row for `French` (id 43197).
- That is 1,792 numbers in total; no other weight was touched.

**Why it works**
1. **The model already knew the translations.** With 10 examples in the prompt, its first output token was right about 85–90% of the time. With no examples, the "Input/Output" wording gave 0%: it predicted a space, repeated the English word, or said true/false. So the problem was the framing, not missing knowledge.
2. **One wording already worked zero-shot.** On the unedited model, `English: cold\nFrench:` got about 90% of first tokens right. It also produced exactly the bare French word followed by a newline.
3. **The two prompts line up token for token.** `Input: x\nOutput:` splits into `[Input][:][x…][\n][Output][:]`, and `[English][:][x…][\n][French][:]` has the same shape. After copying the two rows, the model computes exactly the same thing on the test prompt as on the English/French prompt.

**Results with full 6-token generation**
| Set | Accuracy | Wrong answers |
|---|---|---|
| Training examples | 14/16 | autumn→hiver, old→ancien |
| My own 48 common-word pairs (similar to the training words) | 42/48 | e.g. salt→sal, small→petite, yesterday→demain, cheese→chèvre |
| A broader 64-word list | 48/64 (49 if "oeil" counts for "œil") | e.g. new→nouvelle, sometimes→sometimes, egg→omelette |

The remaining errors are mostly the model's own knowledge limits or gender/word-choice variants, so expect roughly 75–88% on the hidden test, depending on how hard its words are.

**Side effects on general language modelling**
- Text that never contains the exact tokens `Input`/`Output` (capitalised, no leading space) is processed exactly as before. On 64 generic passages, per-token loss changed only in the 3 that contain them.
- Those 3 passages did get worse, one by a lot: a passage starting "Input: a list of integers\nOutput: …" now reads to the model as "English: … / French: …" and expects French. Any edit that makes this format trigger translation would hurt such text to some degree.
- Because input and output embeddings share the same weights, the model now gives `Input`/`Output` exactly the same output scores as `English`/`French`. Where one of those words is likely next (e.g. "Paris (French: …"), the probability is now shared between two tokens. That costs at most about 0.7 nats on those rare tokens.

**What I tried and dropped**
- **Steering vectors built from 10-example prompts:** I averaged the difference in attention outputs between the 10-example and no-example runs at the last prompt position and added it at every layer. In simulation this reached 94% / 75% first-token accuracy on two 16-word sets in the original wording. But it only made multi-token words come out right if also added at each generated token, which would need a detector built into every layer. Added on top of the embedding swap, it made things worse (54/64 vs 57/64 first tokens).
- **Blending the "English"/"French" embeddings with " word":** this was meant to imitate "French word:", but the model then just copied the English word (0%).
- **The "English word / French word" wording itself:** it gave only a noisy gain of about 2 words out of 128, so it wasn't worth building.
